summary: A proposal from Jon Postel to change the Telnet protocol. He suggests dropping the idea of a minimal implementation, removing the DATA TYPE signals, and removing the HIDE YOUR INPUT signal. He argues for each change and says that if no strong objection arrives by May 15 the changes would be assumed wanted.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 328 proposes three changes to Telnet: require a complete standard implementation, remove DATA TYPE signals, and remove HIDE YOUR INPUT. The author says silence by 15 May 1972 would count as support, but the memo does not report the final result.

tldr.problem: The author argues that Telnet's minimum implementation, DATA TYPE signals, and HIDE YOUR INPUT signal were unnecessary or difficult to use consistently.
tldr.mechanism: Jon Postel proposes dropping the minimum implementation concept, eliminating DATA TYPE signals, and removing HIDE YOUR INPUT.
tldr.outcome: The memo says the changes would be assumed desirable if no substantial negative response arrived by 15 May 1972. It does not state the final decision.

sections.title: Three Suggested Changes
sections.content:
Jon Postel proposes three changes to the Telnet protocol. First, drop the idea of a “minimum” implementation and require a standard implementation that includes all aspects of the protocol. Second, eliminate the DATA TYPE signals. Third, remove the HIDE YOUR INPUT signal.

The memo says that if no substantial negative response arrives by 15 May 1972, the changes will be assumed desired and should be incorporated into any Official Telnet Protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo proposes three changes to Telnet and sets a deadline for objections. It does not say what decision was ultimately made.

sections.title: Why Remove the Minimum Implementation
sections.content:
The author argues that accepting an implementation that leaves out part of the protocol implies that the omitted parts are not useful or are not expected to be used. The author also argues that other mechanisms would be built to provide those functions.

On that basis, the memo proposes having one standard implementation that includes the whole protocol rather than defining a minimum subset.
sections.plainLanguage: The author says a permitted partial implementation suggests that the excluded features are not needed or will be handled elsewhere. The proposal is to define only a complete standard implementation.

sections.title: Why Remove DATA TYPE and HIDE YOUR INPUT
sections.content:
The DATA TYPE signals are intended to let communicating processes switch from ASCII to another code set. The author argues that the suggested code sets do not allow Telnet signals, so Telnet would no longer apply after the switch and the protocol provides no way to return to ASCII or Telnet.

HIDE YOUR INPUT is intended to tell the user's Telnet process to hide subsequent input. The memo argues that it is difficult to know how much input to hide and to find a method that works for all combinations of systems and terminals. The author concludes that the signal does not help in a useful way.
sections.plainLanguage: The author argues that DATA TYPE can switch Telnet into a format with no defined way back. HIDE YOUR INPUT does not say how much input to hide or how every terminal should do it.
